extracted.intended_audience: early-career mathematicians and mathematical researchers writing research articles (graduate students, postdocs, faculty)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidelines for planning, composing, and polishing mathematical research papers and expository articles, focused on clarity, structure, notation, and community practices. Emphasizes decisions authors should make (audience, outline, notation), how to present results and proofs, and how to avoid common pitfalls.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose an audience
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide who you hope will read the article and imagine a specific person as your reader.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask: What is your reader's background? What motivation will they need to put your results in context? How much detail would they appreciate seeing in an argument? Grounding choices in a concrete imagined reader helps set level, notation, and amount of explanation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make a detailed outline
rubrics_metrics.description: Begin with a plan for sections, main lemmas, and theorems before filling in proofs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An initial outline may need reorganization as details are added; be ready to 'ruthlessly revise'. Explaining your work to a friend helps form a clear outline and identify big-picture and highlight elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be prepared to ruthlessly revise
rubrics_metrics.description: Expect to reorganize and substantially edit drafts as you develop proofs and details.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adding detail often forces structural changes; revise iteratively and be willing to change notation or sectioning. Consider rewriting drafts from scratch if helpful (anecdote of Serre).

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose notation well
rubrics_metrics.description: Select externally and internally consistent notation, using standard symbols when possible and related names for related objects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bad notation easily loses readers. When collaborating or changing notation, use LaTeX macros rather than find-and-replace to avoid mistakes. Prefer conventional notation in the field and keep related names consistent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Get to the point in the introduction
rubrics_metrics.description: Showcase your main new results as soon as possible in the introduction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It's acceptable to postpone some definitions to a later Notation section if most readers can read the introduction without them. The introduction is often the only part many readers see—treat it as a sales pitch.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make your results stand out
rubrics_metrics.description: Make main results easy to find and scan in the introduction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use theorem environments or separate paragraphs so busy readers can quickly scan for main results; avoid hiding main theorems in the middle of paragraphs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Place your results in context
rubrics_metrics.description: Explain how your work fits with, diverges from, and contributes to prior approaches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Highlight novel contributions and the broader landscape. Use MathSciNet and Google Scholar to find related work; be generous in citing related articles to help readers situate your results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paint a clear roadmap
rubrics_metrics.description: Outline the remaining sections and highlight main arguments and how they fit together.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A roadmap gives readers a canvas to sketch the paper's structure; indicate what each section does and the flow between them to aid comprehension in lengthy technical articles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Introduce each section
rubrics_metrics.description: Begin every section with a sentence indicating what will be done in that section.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Doing so reorients the reader and helps them place the section in the larger argument (serves as internal landmarks).

rubrics_metrics.name: Highlight hypotheses
rubrics_metrics.description: Make clear where each hypothesis is being used in proofs and motivate hypotheses when possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Point out which steps rely on which assumptions; provide counterexamples showing what can fail if assumptions are removed, to motivate necessity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include a running example
rubrics_metrics.description: Use one or two well-chosen examples throughout the article to illustrate ideas and anchor unfamiliar readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Running examples help digest new concepts, illustrate main ideas of long technical arguments, and save readers the effort of reorienting to new examples repeatedly. If unsure, use the minimal interesting example you worked out while proving the result.

rubrics_metrics.name: Break up long arguments
rubrics_metrics.description: Subdivide long proofs into lemmas and smaller pieces to reduce what readers must hold in mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It's acceptable to use a lemma only once; the goal is to minimize cognitive load. Breaking proofs into parts clarifies logic and reduces working-memory demands.

rubrics_metrics.name: Say what to remember and what to forget
rubrics_metrics.description: Indicate which theorems/lemmas are used later and which are local so readers know what to retain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly state when a result is the only one needed later versus when it's not, to free readers' working memory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep theorem statements short (within reason)
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid cluttered, overly long theorem statements so readers can quickly grasp what is being proved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To reduce clutter: (a) define terms before the theorem; (b) isolate complicated technical hypotheses in a separate labeled environment. But include hypotheses that are not global standing assumptions near the theorem—don't sacrifice clarity for brevity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep sentences simple
rubrics_metrics.description: Write sentences that express a single idea to improve readability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine sentences only when it clarifies logic. Prefer readability and clarity over literary flow; short, possibly choppy sentences are acceptable in math writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Start proofs with a warm-up
rubrics_metrics.description: When proofs have easy and hard parts, do the easier parts first to build intuition and momentum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Warm-ups help readers understand techniques and prepare them for the harder steps, especially when parts share ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipate what readers will forget
rubrics_metrics.description: When a definition hasn't been used for a while, give a reference or include it again; use a notation section.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Readers may not recall earlier definitions; remind them or direct them to notation sections to reduce confusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid clutter (minimize extraneous symbols)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use extra symbols only when they help parsing; minimize parentheses and unnecessary multiplication symbols.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: write log x rather than log(x) where appropriate; omit centered dot for multiplication unless needed. Avoid unnecessary notation that burdens the reader.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use figures and diagrams appropriately
rubrics_metrics.description: Supplement written arguments with schematics or diagrams when helpful, ensuring the written argument stands alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be careful with colors (avoid red/green combos; consult palette guides for colorblind accessibility). Write the full argument first and then add figures—do not rely on a picture to replace a rigorous explanation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Declare your variables
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduce new notation before using it in a formula so readers don't need to backtrack.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid constructions like '...where x is...' appended to a sentence; instead, state 'Let x be ...' before formulas. When editing, search for phrases like ', where' and rephrase.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid unnecessary proofs by contradiction
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer direct proofs or contrapositives when possible, as proofs by contradiction complicate tracking assumptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a proof by contradiction is unavoidable, put the subargument in its own paragraph or lemma so the temporary hypothesis is isolated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain the 'obvious'
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not use words like 'clear', 'obvious', or 'trivial' as the sole justification; give at least a sentence of explanation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explaining seemingly trivial steps often takes a sentence and helps avoid errors; overuse of 'clearly' can mask false statements (anecdote about Joe Harris).

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't leave your reader hanging
rubrics_metrics.description: When a claim in a sentence will be justified later, signal that by phrasing such as ', as we now explain.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure that at the end of a sentence the reader either knows why claims are true or is told that an explanation will follow; avoid dangling assertions with no guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clearly connect reasons and conclusions
rubrics_metrics.description: Make explicit which sentences provide reasons and which are conclusions; if an assertion needs a long explanation, turn it into a lemma.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a single assertion takes many sentences to justify, separate it structurally (lemma) or otherwise mark which parts are the supporting reasoning to avoid confusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarify your quantifiers
rubrics_metrics.description: Resolve implicit quantifiers to avoid ambiguity between 'for some' and 'for all'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expressions like 'We have x^2 + 1 in S for x in R' are ambiguous; state quantifiers explicitly to prevent multiple readings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit usage of pronouns
rubrics_metrics.description: Use pronouns like 'it' sparingly and ensure their referents are unambiguous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Overuse of pronouns leads to confusion; name the object instead of relying on 'it' when clarity would suffer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware of not-quite synonyms (prepositions and small words)
rubrics_metrics.description: Be careful with small words like 'so', 'for', 'as', and 'per' because subtle differences have serious mathematical implications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: use 'so that' for purpose and 'such that' for imposing a condition; avoid using 'as' for 'since' because 'as' has many meanings; do not use 'per' for 'by'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid misplaced modifiers
rubrics_metrics.description: Place modifiers (e.g., 'only') as close as possible to the word they modify to prevent unintended readings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'This set only contains the zero vector' is ambiguous; restructure to make the intended meaning clear.

rubrics_metrics.name: State precisely what you actually prove
rubrics_metrics.description: When stating that two objects are isomorphic, specify a map and claim it is an isomorphism rather than merely saying 'they are isomorphic'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specifying maps yields a stronger and more usable statement and prevents ambiguity about what structure or map is intended.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use a single numbering system
rubrics_metrics.description: Employ a consistent numbering scheme for theorems, lemmas, propositions, etc., so statements are easy to find.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example LaTeX setup using amsart: define theorem numbering by section and share numbering across lemma and proposition to avoid citation issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cite precisely
rubrics_metrics.description: Give precise references (theorem numbers, page numbers) and version information for preprints, arXiv, software, and code.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For arXiv preprints include version numbers or dates; for web preprints include URLs and download dates; include software version numbers so readers can locate the exact referenced material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structure sentences to avoid symbols as verbs
rubrics_metrics.description: Write the main verb in words rather than using mathematical symbols as the verb of a sentence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid splitting sentence subjects across formulas and text (example: avoid using '=' as the verb in the natural-language sentence; replace with 'equals'). This improves parseability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Punctuate displayed equations like inline math
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the same punctuation rules for sentences containing displayed equations as for those with inline equations; end displayed equations that finish sentences with a period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The line before a displayed equation often does not need to end with a colon; ensure punctuation is consistent and correct around displays.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not use abbreviations like WLOG, iff, s.t.
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid shorthand abbreviations in prose; write out the English words for logical symbols unless used in formal logic expressions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'without loss of generality', 'if and only if', 'such that', 'for all' etc., in regular prose to maintain accessibility and avoid obscurity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not start a sentence with a symbol
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid beginning sentences with mathematical symbols as they can be missed by readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Start sentences with words; if a formula needs to begin a sentence, rephrase to put words first to signal sentence start clearly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalization of theorem/definition/section
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize words like 'Theorem', 'Definition', or 'Section' only when referring to them by number.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use lowercase when speaking generically (e.g., 'the theorem we just proved') and uppercase when using a label (e.g., 'Theorem 2.1').

rubrics_metrics.name: Use numerals for numbers in math papers
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer numerals for numbers representing mathematical quantities; small counting numbers may be spelled out when not mathematical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'consider two genus 2 curves...' uses numerals when the number is mathematical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not hyphenate common 'non' prefixes
rubrics_metrics.description: Common prefixes like 'non' before math words usually do not need a hyphen (e.g., nonempty, nontrivial).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow common mathematical convention to avoid unnecessary hyphenation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cite forthcoming work only if preprint exists
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not cite 'forthcoming' work unless a publicly available preprint exists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This aligns with AMS Ethical Guidelines and prevents referencing results that readers cannot access; ensures announced but unpublished results are verifiable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid microaggressions and 'microslights' in exposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Be mindful that skipping explanations or dismissing steps as trivial can deter readers, especially those prone to self-doubt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When omitting routine details, use phrases like 'a standard calculation involving ... shows ...' to convey novelty and direct readers, rather than brushing steps off as 'obvious'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enlist feedback and take breaks during revision
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a second pair of eyes and step away from drafts to gain perspective and improve clarity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Revision can be lengthy and iterative; solicit feedback from colleagues, and consider rewriting drafts or letting drafts sit before re-editing to improve clarity and catch errors.
